--- description-meta: High-performance graph analysis library open-graph: title: Traversals | Edgecase description: High-performance graph analysis library twitter-card: title: Traversals | Edgecase description: High-performance graph analysis library gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} - >- ``{=html} title: Traversals guide-section: "Working with graphs" bread-crumbs: false --- Many questions about a graph are questions about moving through it. What does this course lead to? Whose friends are my friends' friends? Which services fail if this one goes down? EdgeCase answers them at three levels: - **neighbor lookups** return the nodes next to a node, - **searches** such as breadth-first and depth-first search explore everything a node can reach, and - **selection traversals** move the graph's current [selection](selections.qmd) along its edges, one step at a time, so that the nodes or edges reached can be acted on. This page covers all three, and ends with ways of drawing a search or traversal step by step. ## A running example Directed graphs are where traversals are most interesting, since the direction of each edge matters. The examples on this page use a small graph of course prerequisites, in which an edge from one course to another means that the first must be taken before the second: ::: {#10081905 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec courses = ec.Graph.from_edges( [ ("Calculus I", "Calculus II"), ("Calculus II", "Multivariable Calculus"), ("Calculus II", "Probability"), ("Linear Algebra", "Machine Learning"), ("Probability", "Statistics"), ("Statistics", "Machine Learning"), ("Programming", "Data Structures"), ("Data Structures", "Algorithms"), ("Data Structures", "Machine Learning"), ("Multivariable Calculus", "Machine Learning"), ("Algorithms", "Capstone"), ("Machine Learning", "Capstone"), ], directed=True, graph_name="Prerequisites", ) courses ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` Name of Graph : Prerequisites Number of nodes : 11 Number of edges : 12 Directed : True Density : 0.11 Average degree (min, max) : 2.18 (1, 5) Strongly connected : False Weakly connected : True Number of strongly connected components : 11 Number of weakly connected components : 1 ``` ::: ::: The traversal methods return node IDs, which are compact but hard to read. A small helper turns a list of IDs into course names: ::: {#3060fcb2 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} def names(ids): return [courses.get_label_from_id(i) for i in ids] ``` ::: A drawing helps to follow the examples. Since a prerequisite graph has no cycles, its courses can be arranged in levels, with each course above everything it depends on. [`topological_generations()`](../reference/Graph.topological_generations.qmd) computes the levels, and [`layout_multipartite()`](../reference/Graph.layout_multipartite.qmd) stacks them: ::: {#47fb83b7 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} generations = courses.topological_generations() courses.set_node_attrs("level", {node: i for i, gen in enumerate(generations) for node in gen}) courses.layout_multipartite(subset_key="level", align="horizontal") courses.plot(layout="pos", label_by="label", node_size=10, height=450) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: The introductory courses with no prerequisites (Calculus I, Linear Algebra, and Programming) sit at the bottom, and the Capstone, which depends directly or indirectly on everything, sits at the top. [Layouts](layouts.qmd) has more on positioning nodes this way. ## Neighbors [`get_neighbors()`](../reference/Graph.get_neighbors.qmd) returns the IDs of the nodes adjacent to a node. In a directed graph, `mode=` chooses the direction: `"out"` (the default) follows edges forward to a node's successors, `"in"` follows them backward to its predecessors, and `"all"` does both: ::: {#e1c6403c .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} names(courses.get_neighbors("Data Structures", mode="out")), names(courses.get_neighbors("Data Structures", mode="in")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` (['Algorithms', 'Machine Learning'], ['Programming']) ``` ::: ::: Data Structures leads to Algorithms and Machine Learning, and requires Programming. In an undirected graph the three modes give the same result. For directed graphs, [`get_successors()`](../reference/Graph.get_successors.qmd) and [`get_predecessors()`](../reference/Graph.get_predecessors.qmd) are dedicated alternatives. They return each neighbor once, even when parallel edges join two nodes, and `get_predecessors()` is faster than `get_neighbors(mode="in")` on large graphs. Machine Learning is the course with the most prerequisites: ::: {#61e40010 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} names(courses.get_predecessors("Machine Learning")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ``` ['Linear Algebra', 'Statistics', 'Data Structures', 'Multivariable Calculus'] ``` ::: ::: Two more lookups compare neighborhoods. [`get_common_neighbors()`](../reference/Graph.get_common_neighbors.qmd) returns the nodes adjacent to both of two nodes, ignoring direction, and [`get_non_neighbors()`](../reference/Graph.get_non_neighbors.qmd) returns every node that isn't adjacent to a given node. Both are building blocks for link prediction, where the nodes that share many neighbors but aren't yet joined are the likeliest new links. In the karate club, the instructor (ID 1) and the administrator (ID 34) aren't friends, but they have four friends in common: ::: {#01286741 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} karate = ec.karate_club() karate.get_common_neighbors(1, 34) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ``` [32, 9, 20, 14] ``` ::: ::: ## Searching A search starts at a node and explores everything reachable from it. [`bfs()`](../reference/Graph.bfs.qmd) does a breadth-first search, which visits all of a node's neighbors before any of theirs, and so works outward in rings of increasing distance. [`dfs()`](../reference/Graph.dfs.qmd) does a depth-first search, which follows each path as far as it goes before backing up. With `return_list=True`, both return the nodes in the order they were visited: ::: {#df5b1811 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} names(courses.bfs("Calculus I", return_list=True)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ``` ['Calculus I', 'Calculus II', 'Multivariable Calculus', 'Probability', 'Machine Learning', 'Statistics', 'Capstone'] ``` ::: ::: ::: {#4320e7c4 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} names(courses.dfs("Calculus I", return_list=True)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ``` ['Calculus I', 'Calculus II', 'Multivariable Calculus', 'Machine Learning', 'Capstone', 'Probability', 'Statistics'] ``` ::: ::: Both searches reach the same seven courses, but in different orders. The breadth-first search visits Multivariable Calculus and Probability, the two courses that Calculus II leads to, one after the other. The depth-first search goes straight from Multivariable Calculus up through Machine Learning to the Capstone, and only then backs up to visit Probability and Statistics. Without `return_list=True`, the methods follow the convention of the other algorithms and store their result as a node attribute: `bfs_order` or `dfs_order`, holding each node's position in the visit order, counted from 0. The four courses that Calculus I doesn't lead to are left without a value, and sort to the end: ::: {#4814d8cb .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} courses.bfs("Calculus I").get_node_df().select("label", "bfs_order").sort("bfs_order", nulls_last=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ### Distances from a source [`bfs_layers()`](../reference/Graph.bfs_layers.qmd) groups the nodes a breadth-first search reaches by their distance from the start: the first list holds the start itself, the second its neighbors, the third the nodes two steps away, and so on: ::: {#9a5aa398 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} [names(layer) for layer in courses.bfs_layers("Calculus I")] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=11} ``` [['Calculus I'], ['Calculus II'], ['Multivariable Calculus', 'Probability'], ['Machine Learning', 'Statistics'], ['Capstone']] ``` ::: ::: Machine Learning is three steps from Calculus I, by way of Multivariable Calculus, and the Capstone four. Statistics is also three steps away, but the longer route from it to Machine Learning doesn't matter: each node belongs to the layer of its shortest distance. When only one ring is needed, [`descendants_at_distance()`](../reference/Graph.descendants_at_distance.qmd) returns it as a set. Its `mode=` argument works as in `get_neighbors()`, so in the karate club, where the default `"out"` is the same as `"all"`, this gives the friends of the instructor's friends who aren't friends of the instructor: ::: {#daac0337 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} len(karate.descendants_at_distance(1, distance=2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=12} ``` 9 ``` ::: ::: Nine members are exactly two steps from the instructor. ### Everything upstream and downstream [`descendants()`](../reference/Graph.descendants.qmd) returns every node reachable from a node, and [`ancestors()`](../reference/Graph.ancestors.qmd) every node that can reach it. For the prerequisite graph, these answer the two most common questions: what does a course open up, and what does it require? ::: {#3da0fa75 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} names(sorted(courses.descendants("Calculus II"))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=13} ``` ['Multivariable Calculus', 'Probability', 'Machine Learning', 'Statistics', 'Capstone'] ``` ::: ::: ::: {#bfb19335 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} names(sorted(courses.ancestors("Machine Learning"))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=14} ``` ['Calculus I', 'Calculus II', 'Multivariable Calculus', 'Probability', 'Linear Algebra', 'Statistics', 'Programming', 'Data Structures'] ``` ::: ::: Machine Learning builds, directly or indirectly, on eight of the other ten courses. Neither result includes the course itself. These methods follow edge direction. To ignore it, and find every node in the same weakly connected component, use [`reachable_nodes()`](../reference/Graph.reachable_nodes.qmd). For a question about one pair of nodes, [`has_path()`](../reference/Graph.has_path.qmd) answers it directly, and when the same fixed graph must answer many such questions, [`reachability_index()`](../reference/Graph.reachability_index.qmd) builds an index once and then answers each query without searching: ::: {#b971fc30 .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} reaches = courses.reachability_index() reaches("Programming", "Capstone"), reaches("Probability", "Algorithms") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=15} ``` (True, False) ``` ::: ::: Programming is a prerequisite, through Data Structures, for the Capstone, but Probability has nothing to do with Algorithms. Build the index after the graph is complete, since it doesn't see later changes. ### Search trees and edge orders A search does more than visit nodes: each node it reaches is discovered along one particular edge. Those edges form a tree, and following it from the root gives a fewest-steps path to every node the search reached. [`bfs_edges()`](../reference/Graph.bfs_edges.qmd) returns the tree's edges as `(parent, child)` pairs, and [`bfs_tree()`](../reference/Graph.bfs_tree.qmd) and [`dfs_tree()`](../reference/Graph.dfs_tree.qmd) return the whole tree as a new directed graph: ::: {#53bdaac3 .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} tree = courses.bfs_tree("Calculus I") tree.count_nodes(), tree.count_edges(), tree.is_arborescence() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=16} ``` (7, 6, True) ``` ::: ::: The tree has the seven courses reachable from Calculus I and one edge into each of them except the root, which makes it an *arborescence*, a directed tree in which every edge points away from the root. (`is_tree()` is for undirected trees, and returns `False` for any directed graph.) The edge from Statistics to Machine Learning is missing: the search reached Machine Learning first from Multivariable Calculus, so that is the edge the tree keeps. A few more methods expose other parts of a search, mostly for building algorithms of your own: | Method | Returns | |---|---| | [`bfs_predecessors()`](../reference/Graph.bfs_predecessors.qmd), [`bfs_successors()`](../reference/Graph.bfs_successors.qmd) | each node's parent, or each node's children, in the BFS tree | | [`dfs_postorder_nodes()`](../reference/Graph.dfs_postorder_nodes.qmd) | the nodes in the order a depth-first search finishes with them | | [`dfs_labeled_edges()`](../reference/Graph.dfs_labeled_edges.qmd) | every step of a depth-first search, labelled `"forward"`, `"nontree"`, or `"reverse"` | | [`edge_bfs()`](../reference/Graph.edge_bfs.qmd), [`edge_dfs()`](../reference/Graph.edge_dfs.qmd) | every reachable *edge*, each visited once, as `(source, target, edge_id)` | | [`bfs_beam_edges()`](../reference/Graph.bfs_beam_edges.qmd) | the edges of a beam search, which keeps only the best few nodes at each level | ## Traversing selections Searches return results. *Selection traversals* move the graph's current selection instead, which makes them a natural partner for the `_ws` methods: select a starting point, traverse to the nodes or edges of interest, and then tag, delete, or extract them. | Method | Moves the selection | |---|---| | [`trav_out()`](../reference/Graph.trav_out.qmd) | from the selected nodes to their successors | | [`trav_in()`](../reference/Graph.trav_in.qmd) | from the selected nodes to their predecessors | | [`trav_both()`](../reference/Graph.trav_both.qmd) | from the selected nodes to all their neighbors | | [`trav_out_edge()`](../reference/Graph.trav_out_edge.qmd) | from the selected nodes to their outgoing edges | | [`trav_in_edge()`](../reference/Graph.trav_in_edge.qmd) | from the selected nodes to their incoming edges | | [`trav_reverse_edge()`](../reference/Graph.trav_reverse_edge.qmd) | from the selected edges to the edges running the opposite way | | [`trav_out_until()`](../reference/Graph.trav_out_until.qmd), [`trav_in_until()`](../reference/Graph.trav_in_until.qmd) | forward or backward, step by step, until nodes meet a condition | Each node traversal *replaces* the selection with the nodes it reaches, so the starting nodes drop out unless they are reached themselves. Chaining traversals walks the selection through the graph one step at a time. Here it starts at Programming and takes two steps forward: ::: {#93f735b6 .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} courses.select_nodes_by_id([courses.get_id_from_label("Programming")], set_op="replace") names(sorted(courses.trav_out().get_selected_node_ids())) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=17} ``` ['Data Structures'] ``` ::: ::: ::: {#58a15e62 .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} names(sorted(courses.trav_out().get_selected_node_ids())) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=18} ``` ['Machine Learning', 'Algorithms'] ``` ::: ::: One step leads to Data Structures, and the next to the two courses that build on it. In an undirected graph, `trav_out()`, `trav_in()`, and `trav_both()` all move to every neighbor. ### From nodes to edges `trav_out_edge()` and `trav_in_edge()` move from a node selection to an edge selection. Continuing from the previous example, this selects the edges into Algorithms and Machine Learning, which are every prerequisite link those two courses have, and marks them in the edge table: ::: {#efb3ded7 .cell execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} ( courses .trav_in_edge() .set_edge_attrs_ws(rel="required_for_advanced") .clear_selection() .get_edge_df() .filter(rel="required_for_advanced") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=19} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: Of the five edges, four lead into Machine Learning and one into Algorithms. `trav_reverse_edge()` works on edge selections only. For each selected edge from `A` to `B`, it selects the edges from `B` back to `A`, which is how to find reciprocated relationships, such as mutual follows or two-way trade, in a directed graph. A prerequisite graph has no reciprocated edges, so it would select nothing here. ### Multi-hop patterns Chained traversals express multi-hop questions compactly. In the karate club, these are the members who are within two steps of the instructor (ID 1) but not friends of the instructor: ::: {#670a916a .cell execution_count=20} ``` {.python .cell-code} ( karate .select_nodes_by_id([1], set_op="replace") .trav_both() .trav_both() .select_nodes_in_neighborhood(1, k=1, set_op="difference") .count_selected_nodes() ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=20} ``` 9 ``` ::: ::: The two traversals reach the nodes two steps from the instructor. The second step also comes back to the instructor and to those of their friends who are friends with one another, so the final selector subtracts the instructor and all of their friends. The count matches the `descendants_at_distance()` result above. ### Traversing until a condition holds `trav_out_until()` and `trav_in_until()` take repeated steps until they reach nodes that satisfy a condition. The condition is a Python function that receives a node ID and returns `True` or `False`. Each selected node advances one step at a time, and stops when it reaches a node that satisfies the condition; that node then becomes part of the result. To use the course levels for this, give each course a number in the usual university style, where 100-level courses are introductory and 400-level the most advanced: ::: {#d3d0e190 .cell execution_count=21} ``` {.python .cell-code} course_level = { "Calculus I": 100, "Linear Algebra": 100, "Programming": 100, "Calculus II": 200, "Data Structures": 200, "Multivariable Calculus": 300, "Probability": 300, "Statistics": 300, "Algorithms": 300, "Machine Learning": 400, "Capstone": 400, } courses.set_node_attrs("course_level", course_level) def advanced(level): return lambda node: courses.get_node(node).attributes["course_level"] >= level ``` ::: This finds the first upper-level course on each path out of Calculus I and Programming: ::: {#1f4cd1be .cell execution_count=22} ``` {.python .cell-code} ( courses .select_nodes_by_id([1, 8], set_op="replace") .trav_out_until(advanced(300)) ) names(sorted(courses.get_selected_node_ids())) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=22} ``` ['Multivariable Calculus', 'Probability', 'Machine Learning', 'Algorithms'] ``` ::: ::: The paths from Calculus I end at Multivariable Calculus and Probability, and the paths from Programming at Algorithms and Machine Learning (since Machine Learning, at the 400 level, also passes the test). Data Structures and Calculus II, at the 200 level, were passed over on the way. Two arguments change what ends up selected. `add_to_selection=True` keeps the starting nodes, and `exclude_unmatched=False` keeps every node visited along the way, rather than only those that satisfy the condition. Together they select a whole route, here every course on the way from Calculus I to the first 400-level course: ::: {#ceb15c5e .cell execution_count=23} ``` {.python .cell-code} ( courses .select_nodes_by_id([1], set_op="replace") .trav_out_until(advanced(400), add_to_selection=True, exclude_unmatched=False) ) names(sorted(courses.get_selected_node_ids())) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=23} ``` ['Calculus I', 'Calculus II', 'Multivariable Calculus', 'Probability', 'Machine Learning', 'Statistics'] ``` ::: ::: The search stops after `max_steps=` steps (30 by default), which guards against running forever around a cycle in which no node matches. ## Drawing a search Two methods draw a search or traversal as an animation, which helps with teaching, with explaining an analysis, and with checking that a traversal does what was intended. Both return a step player, an interactive drawing with controls for stepping forward and back through the search. In a notebook or a rendered document it displays itself, and its `save()` method writes it to an HTML file. `plot_traversal()` animates a breadth-first or depth-first search. Given only a `source=` node, it runs a breadth-first search from it, and lights up the nodes in the order they are reached: ::: {#16812e88 .cell execution_count=24} ``` {.python .cell-code} courses.clear_selection().plot_traversal(source="Calculus I", algorithm="BFS", seed=1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=24} ```{=html}
Step 0 / 7
BFS traversal — 7 nodes
``` ::: ::: To animate another search, pass its visit order as `visit_order=`, and optionally its tree edges as `tree_edges=` (as `(parent, child)` pairs, such as those from `bfs_edges()`). `record_traversal()` records a sequence of selection operations instead. It returns a recorder that offers the same `select_*`, `trav_*`, `deselect_*`, `invert_*`, and `clear_selection()` methods as the graph. Each call is applied to the graph and logged, and the recorder's `plot()` method replays the log, highlighting the selection after each step: ::: {#9739d4e9 .cell execution_count=25} ``` {.python .cell-code} recorder = courses.record_traversal() ( recorder .select_nodes_by_id([courses.get_id_from_label("Programming")]) .trav_out() .trav_out() .trav_out() ) [step["ids"] for step in recorder.steps] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=25} ``` [[8], [9], [10, 6], [11]] ``` ::: ::: The `steps` attribute holds the log as a list of dictionaries, one per operation, each with the operation's name and the IDs selected after it. The three steps out of Programming reach Data Structures, then Algorithms and Machine Learning, and finally the Capstone: ::: {#4817cbbe .cell execution_count=26} ``` {.python .cell-code} recorder.plot(node_size=12, seed=1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=26} ```{=html}
